identity.title: Is Your LLM Overcharging You? Tokenization, Transparency, and Incentives

problem.claim: The paper examines whether pay-per-token cloud pricing gives model providers incentives to misreport token usage and overcharge users.

gap.claim: Users cannot prove, or even know, whether providers are overcharging them under this mechanism.

contributions.claim: Shows that pay-per-token pricing creates a financial incentive for providers to strategize and misreport token counts.
Develops an efficient heuristic that can significantly overcharge users without raising suspicion, with stated operating cost below the added revenue.

Shows that eliminating the incentive to strategize requires pricing tokens linearly by character count, and introduces a prescription for maintaining average provider profit margin during the transition.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they introduce a simple profit-margin-preserving prescription for transitioning to incentive-compatible pricing.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that transparent disclosure of the model’s generative process makes optimal suspicion-free misreporting hard for an unfaithful provider.
The authors report that their heuristic enables significant suspicion-free overcharging and costs less to run than the resulting additional revenue.
The authors report experiments using Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models with prompts from a popular benchmarking platform.

narrative_sequence.summary: Specialized hardware and energy requirements have contributed to the popularity of cloud-based LLM services.
Because users pay a fixed price per generated token, providers may benefit from strategically misreporting usage, while users lack proof or knowledge of overcharging.
Transparency about generation makes optimal covert misreporting hard, yet a heuristic proof-of-concept still enables significant suspicion-free overcharging.
The paper argues for character-count-linear token pricing and gives a prescription intended to preserve average provider profit margins.
Experiments are reported with three LLM families and benchmark-platform prompts.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs an incentive analysis, an attack proof-of-concept, a transparency condition, and a pricing redesign.

lessons.interpretation: A strong abstract can connect mechanism, exploitability, mitigation, and redesign so the practical implication follows from the analysis.
lessons.application: Frame a systems-economics paper as: identify the incentive, demonstrate its operational consequence, state a condition that constrains it, then propose a compatible redesign.
lessons.exception: This sequence is unsuitable when the work has no mechanism-level explanation or when mitigation and redesign are outside its scope.

unknowns: The abstract gives no experimental outcomes, sample sizes, baselines, or evaluation protocol beyond model families and prompt source.
The formal meaning of transparency, the proof details, and the scope of the pricing necessity claim are unspecified.
